accepted.question_text: For a given positive integer n, what is the largest possible number K(n) of triangles that can be formed by n straight lines in the plane if only triangles that are nonoverlapping and uncut by any of the lines are counted?

evidence.quote: Problem 1. Determine the largest number K(n) of (nonoverlapping, uncut, see Figure 1) triangles that can be drawn using only n straight lines in the plane.

accepted.question_text: When n = 10 straight lines are used in the Kobon triangle problem, is the best known upper bound non-sharp, or does there exist a configuration of 10 lines in the plane that forms 26 nonoverlapping, uncut triangles?

evidence.quote: Particular case of Problem 1. The best configuration known with 10 lines has 25 triangles. But the bound by Clement and Bader only guarantees that K(10) ≤ 26. Maybe the bound is not tight enough? or it is possible to find a configuration with 10 lines and 26 triangles?

accepted.question_text: Among all plane regions of width 1 that can be moved through a right-angled hallway of width 1 by continuous rigid motions in the plane, which region has the largest possible area?

evidence.quote: Problem 2. Determine the plane region S (from now on and in this section we will call it sofa) of largest area which can be “moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width one” (see below).

Formally, for a parameter t representing time and varying in a closed interval I, we need to find a uniparametric family of rigid motions in the plane Φt such that (1) for every t ∈ I “the sofa is inside the hallway” (Φt(S) ⊂ H) and (2) “the sofa moves continously and without teleportation through the corridor”.

The sofa needs not to be convex. For instance, the shape of the better known solution (its area is approximately 2.2195) reminds to an old telephone (see Figure 4). It was proposed by J. Gerver (see [14] for a precise description) and it is conjectured to be the optimal sofa.

accepted.question_text: A worm is any plane curve of length 1, and a cage is a plane region into which every such worm can be placed by translations and rotations without changing the worm's shape. Does there exist a cage of minimum area for all unit-length worms, and if so, what is that smallest-area cage?

evidence.quote: Problem 3. Define a worm to be any plane curve of length one. Define a cage to be a plane region that can accommodate any worm, that is, the worms have a fixed shape that cannot be altered, but they can be rotated and translated to fix into the region.
Find, if it exists, the cage of smallest area.

As suggested in the statement, the following situation could also be possible: it may exists a value A, such that we can find cages with area as close as we want to A but such that there is no cage of area A.

accepted.question_text: For each positive integer n, what is the smallest triangle that can contain n circles of radius 1 without overlap?

evidence.quote: Problem 4. For each n ∈ N, find the smallest triangle in which you can package n circles of radius 1. By package we mean that the n circles must be completely contained in the the triangle without overlapping.

accepted.question_text: If n is a triangular number, is the smallest equilateral triangle that can contain n - 1 circles of radius 1 exactly the same size as the smallest equilateral triangle that can contain n such circles?

evidence.quote: Particular case of Problem 4. Let n be a triangular number. The smallest equilateral triangle needed to package n − 1 circles of radius 1 and to package n circles of radius 1 is the same.

accepted.question_text: Let F be a known plane region representing a forest. Find a parametrized curve C such that, no matter which point P of F a hiker starts from and no matter which initial direction the hiker faces, every curve congruent to C with initial point P eventually leaves F; among all such guaranteed-escape curves, which one minimizes the worst-case escape time, equivalently the length of the shortest trajectory that guarantees escape?

evidence.quote: Problem 5. Let F be a plane region that we will call forest. Find a parametrized curve C such that (1) for every P ∈ F, for every curve C̃ congruent to C and with initial point P, C̃ “scapes from F” (it is not contained in F) and (2) among them find the “best” possible one.
Here by “best” we will interpret the shortest time of escape in the worst case or, in other words, the shortest trajectory that guarantees to escape.

accepted.question_text: For triangular forests, and in particular for equilateral triangles, what guaranteed-escape curve minimizes the worst-case escape time for a hiker who knows the forest's shape but not the starting point or initial direction?

evidence.quote: The problem is still open for very simple choices of F.
The problems remains unsolved for triangles. There is a conjecture for the best curve for equilateral triangles in [3].

accepted.question_text: Does every Jordan curve in the plane contain four points that are the vertices of a square? Here a Jordan curve is a simple closed curve, and 'inscribes a square' means that the four vertices of the square lie on the curve, without requiring the whole square to lie inside the region bounded by the curve.

evidence.quote: Problem 6. Decide if any Jordan curve inscribes a square.
that the four vertices of the square are contained in the curve, not that the entire square is contained in the interior region (see Figure 11).
But the general question have remained open for more than a century.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Several variations of the initial F-chordal point problem remain open.

evidence.quote: F-chordal point problems (4). The equichordal point problem was first proposed in 1916-17 and solved in 1997 by Rychlik in [33]. This problems asked about existence and uniqueness of curves having two equichordal points, that is, points such that every chord passing through it has the same length. A generalization of equichordal points are F-chordal points, which, for a given curve, satisfy certain relations for the chords passing through them. Several variations of the initial problem remain open.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Show that the circle is the unique C∞ Jordan curve with an equipower point.

evidence.quote: Conjecture about the circle (1). This problem could have been included in the previous family, but it deserves to be highlighted. Show that the circle is the unique C∞ Jordan curve with an equipower point (see [41] for the definition).

needs_review.question_text_raw: Einstein problem concerning aperiodic tilings in the plane.

evidence.quote: Einstein problem (2, 3). It concerns aperiodic tilings in the plane.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Hammer X-ray problem about reconstructing plane regions from chord information.

evidence.quote: Hammer X-ray problem (3). It deals with the number of “ideal tomographic pictures” (with no noise) needed for the identification or reconstruction of plane regions from information about their chords.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Heesch's problem: determine the maximum number of layers of congruent copies of a region that can surround it.

evidence.quote: Heesch’s problem (2,3). For some region D in the plane, determining the maximum number of layers of (congruent) copies of D that can surround it.
